frames.narration: The first version has the card form on the shop's own page, posting to its own server. The number is typed into your page, sent through your web server and API, processed by your payment service and forwarded to the provider. That is 4 of your 8 systems in scope.

To charge returning customers the team stores the number. A log line records the request body, a nightly backup copies the database and an analytics job copies it too. All 8 systems are now in scope, and card numbers sit at rest in 4 places.
An attacker gets hold of one old database dump, or a backup, or a log archive. Any of the four contains full card numbers, so every stored customer card is now usable by the thief.

The team switches to the provider's hosted fields. The customer types the number into fields served by the provider inside your page, and the browser sends it straight to the provider. Your servers never receive it.

The provider puts the number in its vault and returns a token. Your servers keep the token, the last 4 digits, the brand and the expiry. Only the checkout page, which serves the code around the fields, remains in scope: 1 of 8.
The same attacker steals the same kind of database dump. It holds tokens that only work for your account at the provider, so it is of little use. Charging a customer later is a call with the token.

A full redirect goes one step further: the customer pays on the provider's own page and comes back with a result, so no provider code runs inside your page. Your checkout page still decides where the customer is sent, and a tampered page could send them to a fake payment page, so it stays in scope: still 1 of 8, as with hosted fields. The price is less control over the look and flow of checkout.
